This article presents an automatic method to derive the optimal reference frame for the task model directly from recorded motion and wrench data. This frame maximizes decoupling between the learned signals, enabling the design of a decoupled task controller. The method is founded on screw theory, entirely probabilistic and requires no hyperparameters. The method is generic as it works regardless of whether the task involves translation, rotation, force, or moment, or any combination thereof. While other control approaches could be used, we propose a generic, decoupled, constraint-based and velocity-resolved controller to work in tandem with the derived task model. It involves a small number of task-dependent control parameters that need to be tuned. The derivation of the task model, the robustness of the controller, and the task generalization capabilities of their combination were validated for various tasks involving contact between rigid objects, including surface following and manipulation of articulated objects. The results show a good agreement between derived and assumed expert task frames as well as the effectiveness and versatility of the overall approach. 1. JSON: Name: screwframe_taskmodel_pipeline Title: Automatic probabilistic task-frame derivation via screw-theoretic averaging for decoupled learning and control of contact-rich manipulation Short Hypothesis: A probabilistic task-frame derived from demonstration motion and wrench data using screw-theoretic average intersection and orientation operators yields greater decoupling between motion and wrench components and produces statistically lower task execution errors and higher robustness than (a) expert-chosen frames, (b) motion-only or wrench-only orientation selection, and (c) prior candidate-selection TF methods when used with a generic constraint-based controller. Related Work: Existing approaches either require an expert to specify a task frame, select from predefined candidate frames using demonstration data, or derive only partial frame components (orientation or principal directions) from data. Classical geometric methods (average vector orientation, average screw intersection) can estimate orientation or intersection but are applied separately and often normalize vectors or require prior choices. Other works optimize an objective (e.g., mechanical power) numerically to identify frames but need initialization, hyperparameters, and provide limited uncertainty quantification. Task models in learning-from-demonstration typically focus on translation and force or on rotation and moment but rarely combine all six screw components in a single invariant model; controllers used are predominantly hybrid force/position, impedance, or variable-impedance and are often designed per-task. Limitations in prior work include dependence on expert insight, lack of a unified analytical TF derivation that handles both origin and orientation, absence of uncertainty estimates, hyperparameter sensitivity, limited consideration of full wrench-twist coupling, and limited demonstrations of generalization across translation/rotation and force/moment dominated tasks. Abstract: We present a pipeline that automatically derives an invariant task frame from demonstration motion and wrench data and couples that task model with a generic decoupled constraint-based controller for contact-rich manipulation. The method analytically identifies an optimal frame origin by averaging screw-axis intersection estimates and an optimal orientation by averaging dominant direction estimates, combining motion and wrench information in a probabilistic manner and producing uncertainty estimates for both origin and orientation. The task model parametrizes demonstrated pose, twist and wrench trajectories in that frame using a geometry-aligned progress variable. The controller enforces simultaneous pose and wrench constraints as weighted velocity-resolved tasks, enabling robust execution with three task-tunable parameters. The main contribution is a hyperparameter-free, screw-theory-based TF derivation that maximizes decoupling between directional and moment components and between motion and wrench, enabling improved task tracking and generalization across translation/rotation and force/moment dominated tasks. Expected outcomes are reduced execution errors, improved contact robustness, and principled uncertainty information for downstream adaptation. Experiments: Datasets: For evaluation use (A) five human passive-observation demonstrations per task collected with pose tracker + FT sensor for seven representative contact tasks: revolute joint manipulation, peg-on-hole alignment, bottle opening, prismatic joint, drawing (point-on-plane), 2-D contour following, 3-D contour following; (B) robot-collected iterations after initial transfer for selected scenarios; (C) simulated demonstrations (optional) for controlled noise studies. Baselines: (1) expert-chosen TF, (2) motion-only AVOF orientation + ASIP origin, (3) wrench-only ASIP/AVOF, (4) numerical optimization TF (minimize mechanical power), (5) random TF, controller baselines: (a) hybrid force/position tuned per-task, (b) isotropic impedance controller with tuned gains. Metrics: RMSE pose orientation (deg), RMSE position (mm), RMSE twist (deg/s, mm/s), RMSE wrench (N, Nm), task success rate, contact-loss events, convergence time, robustness (error increase under perturbation), statistical significance (paired tests). Experimental setup: UR10e robot with 6-DOF FT sensor and external tracker; use five-demo training per task, derive TF with proposed method, compute time-invariant trajectories via geometric progress variable, execute with the generic constraint-based controller at 100 Hz. Evaluation protocol: run each task for 10 independent trials in nominal setting; perturbations include (i) speed scaled ×{0.25,4.5}, (ii) wrench scaled ×{0.5,3}, (iii) geometry perturbations small (±5–25 mm/deg) and large (replace tool, detach/relocate workpiece), (iv) sensor noise injection (pose/force), (v) TF origin/orientation manual offsets. Ablations: (A) TF derivation ablation: (i) motion-only vs wrench-only vs combined; (ii) mean-subtraction in ASIP (Model 1 vs Model 2 decision) on origin selection; (iii) weighted vs unweighted orientation averaging; (B) controller ablation: (i) pose-only, wrench-only, combined with varying weights; (C) demonstration size: 1 vs 3 vs 5 trials impact. Statistical analysis: paired t-tests or Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (α=0.05) between proposed method and baselines over RMSE and success rate; report effect sizes. Risk Factors and Limitations: The method assumes demonstrations and executions involve predominantly rigid bodies and negligible dynamic wrench components; high inertia or unmodeled dynamics can violate the screw-based assumptions and degrade TF estimates. Quality of derived TF depends on demonstration signal-to-noise ratio; noisy FT or pose measurements, or very few demonstrations, can produce ill-conditioned covariance matrices or ambiguous AVOF/ASIP results. Scenarios with deformable contacts, fluid contacts, or multi-limb multi-contact interactions may invalidate single-screw assumptions and reduce decoupling. The analytical averaging can be ill-defined when orientation candidates differ by 180 degrees, requiring special handling. The proposed isotropic controller does not exploit anisotropic compliance and may be suboptimal for tasks that require direction-specific stiffness; scaling to very high-DoF manipulators or many simultaneous constraints can increase computational load in real time. Transfer across large geometry changes may require iterative re-derivation or human intervention; uncertainty estimates quantify but do not automatically resolve ambiguous TF choices.
